claims.text: Noble-metal precursors such as Pd(II), Pt(II), Rh(III), Ir(IV), and Ru(III) have different reduction kinetics.
One-shot precursor injection causes sequential generation of the constituent metal atoms.
Sequential reduction during one-shot synthesis promotes phase-separated PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals.
Controlled dropwise precursor addition better synchronizes reduction of the individual metal ions.
Synchronized reduction produces simultaneous nucleation and growth.
Dropwise addition produces a more uniform, single-phase solid-solution PdPtRhIrRu HEA nanocrystal than one-shot injection.
Single-phase HEAs retain a random distribution of surface atoms, whereas phase segregation destroys that distribution.
A homogeneous solid-solution structure mediates improved catalytic performance relative to phase-separated structures.
Homogeneous atomic distribution optimizes the electronic structure of surface-active sites.
The optimized surface electronic structure improves adsorption energies of catalytic reaction intermediates.
Improved adsorption energies lead to enhanced catalytic activity.
Single-phase PtPdRhIrRu HEA nanocrystals show higher HER and HOR activity and durability than phase-separated nanocrystals and commercial Pt/C.
Dropwise-produced nanocrystals will have higher HER and HOR performance than otherwise identical one-shot-produced nanocrystals.
The proposed synthesis uses equimolar noble-metal precursors at about 180°C in ethylene glycol with l-ascorbic acid and PVP.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to low-temperature solution syntheses conducted under conditions similar to the cited synthesis.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to high-temperature bulk methods such as arc melting or to non-solution nanoparticle syntheses.
The controlled test compares one-shot and dropwise synthesis of PdPtRhIrRu while holding all other synthesis conditions fixed.
Failure of dropwise addition to improve both phase uniformity and catalytic activity relative to the one-shot control would falsify the hypothesis.
